turns.question: Our pH probe has been in the water two seasons and the readings feel sluggish. After I run a fresh calibration, what number should I be looking at to tell me the electrode itself is still any good, and what counts as passing?
turns.answer:
After calibration, check the **slope** — that's the number that tells you whether the electrode itself is still healthy.

**What to look for:** the calibration slope, reported either as a percentage of the theoretical Nernst slope or in millivolts per pH unit.

**What counts as passing:**
- Slope of **95 to 101 percent** of the theoretical Nernst response, which corresponds to **56.2 to 59.8 mV/pH unit at 25 °C** 【6†"Properly working electrodes should have slopes that are 56.2 to 59.8 mV/pH unit at 25 °C, which is 95 to 101 percent"】.
- The ideal slope at 25 °C is 59.16 mV/pH unit 【3†"The ideal slope of the calibration curve at 25 °C, based on the Nernst equation (see section 2.2), is 59.16 mV/pH unit"】.

**If it fails:** a slope outside 95–101 percent indicates probable electrode deterioration 【12†"slope of less than 95 percent or greater than 101 percent indicates probable electrode deterioration"】. The guidance is to first clean the electrode and check the filling-solution level, that the fill hole is open, and that the junction is free flowing, then recalibrate 【11†"first clean the electrode and check: the level of the filling solution, that the fill hole is open, and that the junction is free flowing; then, recalibrate"】. If it still fails after recalibration, the electrode should be cleaned, reconditioned, or replaced 【7†"Clean, recondition, or replace the electrode if, after recalibration, the slope remains outside the acceptable range of 95 to 101 percent"】.

One more relevant note for your situation: the typical useful life expectancy of pH electrodes in environmental field operation is approximately 12 to 18 months, so a two-season-old electrode is worth watching closely 【19†"the typical useful life expectancy of pH electrodes used in environmental field operation is approximately 12 to 18 months"】. Your sluggish response is also consistent with what the troubleshooting guide lists as a possible cause of slow response, including a clogged or partially clogged junction or a contaminated electrode 【8†"Clogged or partially clogged junction—follow the manufacturer's instructions to unclog the junction"】.

Liquid-Filled Electrodes
If problems persist during calibration of a liquid-filledelectrode, or if there is reason to doubt that the electrode is in
good working condition, check the manufacturer’s instructions
for testing and reconditioning the electrode. Reconditioning
procedures should be implemented if the electrode’s slope
response has deteriorated to less than 95 percent or greater
than 101 percent, if the meter no longer recognizes the pH
buffers because of shifting of the isopotential point, or if the
response time is longer than expected. Document the date,
serial number, and action in the pH-meter/electrode logbook if
the electrode has been reconditioned or replaced. Salt crystal
deposits in the reference electrode or reference junction com-
monly cause pH electrodes to malfunction. The following
general procedure for renewing the filling solution can be used
to attempt to bring a liquid-filled electrode back into proper
working condition. If the electrode has a replaceable reference
junction, follow the manufacturer’s instructions for changing
the reference junction, which may require renewing the filling
solution. If the electrode does not have a replaceable reference
junction, follow the general instructions below to renew the
filling solution.

• Use a small pipet or syringe to remove the filling
solution through the filling hole. Another method of
removing the filling solution is to wick it out with

may have specific recommendations for removing
the filling solution.
2. 	Flush the pH electrode with DIW.
• Use a pipet, syringe, or squeeze bottle to partially fill
the pH electrode chamber with DIW.
• Remove the DIW from the electrode as

3.3 	Electrode Storage
Electrodes must be clean before they are stored for any
length of time. Refer to the manufacturer’s instructions for
the proper short-term (used daily or weekly) and long-term
(months) storage requirements of the electrode.
General guidelines for short-term storage:
• Storage solutions are specific to the type of electrode;
check the manufacturer’s manual for each electrode.
Do not store pH electrodes in DIW unless instructed
to do so by the manufacturer.
• Storage solutions have a limited shelf life. Label
storage-solution containers with the expiration date and
discard expired solutions in an appropriate manner.
• Do not place cotton or paper towel in the electrode cap
to help keep it moist, as this practice can scratch the
glass bulb membrane.
• Store pH electrodes upright so the filling solution or gel
is always in contact with the reference junction.
• Store pH electrodes wet between uses to maximize
their accuracy and response time.
• The glass bulb membrane should be fully immersed in
the proper electrode-storage solution.
• For liquid-filled electrodes, replace the plug on the fill
hole and cover the electrode bulb with the cap between
uses. Fill the cap with enough storage solution to keep
the bulb wet.
• Storing the electrode in either pH-4 or -7 buffer may be
recommended for short-term storage (less than 1 day).
Unless it is recommended by the manufacturer, do not
store the electrode in buffer solution for a long period.
• Gel-filled electrodes should be stored according to the
manufacturer’s instructions.
General guidelines for long-term storage:
• Store electrodes in the appropriate storage solu-
tion and cap as recommended by the manufacturer.

have an isopotential point at pH 7 (the pH at which e.m.f. is
equal to 0 mV). Most modern pH meters are equipped with
ATC, which compensates for the temperature dependence of
the standard buffers. The Nernst equation gives the expected
(theoretical) response potential of the pH buffer at the specific
temperature of the calibration (Hem, 1989), and after calibra-
tion most meters report the calibration slope as a percentage
of the Nernstian theoretical slope. To successfully calibrate
pH instrumentation, (1) the meter and pH electrode must be
functioning properly, (2) the system must be calibrated with
pH buffers so the pH of the solution being measured is within
the calibrated range, and (3) the temperature of the pH buffers
during calibration needs be stable and similar to (within 10 °C
of) the temperature of the solution being measured.
A properly working pH system has—
• new or adequately charged batteries
• a thermistor that functions properly and accurately
measures the temperature
• a pH electrode with an accurate Nernstian response
(slope of 95–101 percent of the theoretical
Nernstian slope)
• an isopotential point near pH 7
• a quick response time (1–2 minutes) in standard
buffer solutions.
Accurate measurement of the pH of environmental
samples requires calibration with pH buffers that bracket the
pH of the sample. Before the pH instrument system is cali-
brated, it is useful to estimate (or anticipate from historical
site data, if available) the pH and conductivity of the waters to
be encountered at the field sites. If no data are available from
which to estimate sample pH, then pH indicator paper can
be used onsite as a gross indicator of the pH of the site, but
under no circumstances should a pH value from indica-
tor paper be recorded as the site pH. A two- or three-point
calibration can be performed. Most manufacturers use a linear
calibration curve for all calibrations (including multipoint
calibrations). For most modern meters, a two-point calibration,
typically with buffers selected from pH 10.01, 7.00, 4.01, or
1.68, is recommended. pH meters that use either a point-to-
point calibration or a nonlinear function are not recommended.
Follow the manufacturer’s instructions with respect to recom-
mended buffers and the sequence of buffer calibration.
Examples: When measuring pH in a stream—
• If pH values are expected to be between 7 and 8,
then the standard pH-7 and pH-10.01 buffers (at a
minimum) should be selected.
• If pH values are expected to be less than 7, then the
standard pH-7 and pH-4.01 buffers (at a minimum)
should be selected.
For the two examples above, a three-point calibration
using pH-4.01, -7.00, and -10.01 buffers could also be used to
allow measurement of a larger range of pH.
The pH of a solution changes with temperature, and most
modern pH meters automatically compensate for temperature
differences between the buffers used for calibration and the
measurements made in samples. However, electrodes may not
behave ideally and this feature should be tested regularly. Cali-

• The millivolt test—For pH meters that display
and store millivolt readings, troubleshoot a suspect
electrode or calibration by using the following
guidelines to determine adequate voltage potentials
for each buffer:
• pH 10.01 buffer: readings between −192 and
−162 mV
• pH 7.00 buffer: readings between −15 and 15 mV
• pH 4.01 buffer: readings between 162 and 192 mV
• pH 1.68 buffer: readings between 300 and 330 mV
• The meter may not recognize the pH buffer or
may incorrectly identify the pH buffer if the mil-
livolt response is outside the acceptable range. The
acceptable range may vary with the manufacturer.
• If buffers other than the standard pH 1.68, 4.01, 7.00,
and 10.01 buffers are used, refer to the information
provided with the specific buffer lot to determine
the correct, temperature-compensated pH value for
that buffer. Buffers other than pH 1.68, 4.01, 7.00,
and 10.01 should be used for calibration only in
cases where expected measured pH is less than 1.68
or greater than 10, or if the pH meter specifically
requires their use.

TECHNICAL NOTE:
After calibration, measure the pH of the final pH buffer and
check that the measured pH at the calibration temperature is
within 0.05 pH units of the certified value (table 6.4–3).
• 	If the measured pH is equal to or within 0.05
pH units of the certified value, proceed with the
sample measurement.
• 	If the measured pH is more than ±0.05 pH units
from the certified value, recalibrate the pH electrode
or determine whether the electrode is not functioning
properly and should be reconditioned or replaced.

The pH of a solution changes with temperature, and most
modern pH meters automatically compensate for temperature
differences between the buffers used for calibration and the
measurements made in samples. However, electrodes may not
behave ideally and this feature should be tested regularly. Cali-
brating a pH meter and electrode with buffers that are within±10 °C of the sample temperature is recommended. This task
can be accomplished by placing the buffers in a mesh bag and
equilibrating them to the temperature of the water at the sam-
pling location before calibration. However, for most sampling
situations, where the temperature of the water is between 5 and
35 °C and the pH is between 4.0 and 9.5, the recommended
procedure is to calibrate the meter in the more controlled
environment of the office laboratory, and then allow the meter
to compensate for temperature differences at the sampling site.
Again, the accuracy of field measurements should be checked
regularly with buffers equilibrated to the environmental-
sample temperatures to verify the readings. If the pH of the
buffers checked at the field site at ±10 °C of the temperature of
the environmental sample is more than ±0.05 pH unit different
from the value the buffer should return at that temperature, the
meter and electrode should be recalibrated at a temperature
that is ±10 °C of the field-measurement temperature.
For multiparameter sondes that will be deployed for
continuous measurements in the field in a range of conditions,
the recommended procedure is to calibrate in the laboratory
and then conduct checks in the field at ambient tempera-
tures to verify the accuracy of the readings. Recalibration
may be necessary if the initial check is more than ±0.05 pH
unit different from the value the buffer should return. If the
measurement temperature is more than ±10 °C different from
the laboratory calibration temperature, checks in the field are
more likely to fail and recalibration may be necessary.

generally apply whenever a pH instrument system is to be
calibrated. Because calibration and operating procedures can
differ with the instrument system, check the manufacturer’s
recommended calibration procedures and calibration buffer

calibration instructions and the more general instructions in

Specific conductance measurements are only as good
as the calibration itself. Several factors must be considered
when calibrating the meter. Thermal expansion of the con-
ductivity cell can affect the cell constant; however, the cell
constants (𝐾cell) of modern field probes are generally stable

chloride (KCl) solutions, and the linear (0.019–0.020) and
nonlinear (International Organization for Standardization,

reliable calibrations from 5 to 35 °C. Caution should be
used when calibrating at temperatures greater than 35 °C,
however, because the commonly used nonlinear (International

sation deviates substantially when applied to KCl solutions.
Therefore, if a modern conductivity probe that expands

water to be measured is between 5 and 35 °C, the temperature

8.0 	Troubleshooting 	19
7.0 	Reporting
Due to the array of reactions that can change the pH in
environmental samples, the effect of temperature on the opera-
tion of the pH instrument system, and easily changed chemical
and microbiological equilibria within the sample, pH measure-
ments are required to be completed and recorded at the field
site in situ or as soon as possible after removing the sample
from the environmental medium.
Most meters measure with precision in the range of ±0.01
units. Modern meters and multiparameter sondes can some-
times discern environmental patterns within this range. There-
fore, pH should be recorded on field sheets to ±0.01 pH units.
Accuracy of pH measurements is greater at lower values of pH
because hydrogen ion activity is greater. Accuracy of pH mea-
surements is poorer at higher values of pH because the activity
of hydrogen ions is lower.
When recording pH—
• Record the method that was used to make the pH
measurement, as well as the date and serial numbers or
other identifiers for the meter and electrode.
• Record environmental measurements on field sheets
and in NWIS to ±0.01 standard pH units, if the meter
provides this level of precision.
• Rounding for reporting purposes will depend on the
accuracy and precision of the equipment and is typi-
cally to three significant figures. Rounding to ±0.01
units at low and neutral ranges of pH, and to ±0.1 units
for pH values equal to or greater than 10.0, is recom-
mended. The accuracy and precision of the readings for
each meter should be defined further with calibration
checks and quality-control sampling.
• Always record temperature with measurements of pH.
8.0 	Troubleshooting
Consult the instrument manufacturer for recommended
troubleshooting actions for specific single-parameter and
multiparameter pH instrument systems. Many problems
encountered during pH calibration and measurement can be
attributed directly to the condition and responsiveness of the
pH electrode. Depending on use, the typical useful life expec-
tancy of pH electrodes used in environmental field operation
is approximately 12 to 18 months. With time, pH electrodes
need to be evaluated more frequently to determine whether
the deviation of the millivolt response slope falls outside the
acceptable response of 95 to 101 percent of the ideal response
slope in NIST-traceable buffers. Replace the pH electrode
when the response falls outside the acceptable range for the
response slope and the deviation cannot be corrected through
cleaning or reconditioning. Also, for any problem encountered,
first check that the instrument batteries are fully charged, and
keep spare fresh batteries on hand.

After calibration, check the **slope** — that's the number that tells you whether the electrode itself is still healthy.

**What to look for:** the calibration slope, reported either as a percentage of the theoretical Nernst slope or in millivolts per pH unit.

**What counts as passing:**
- Slope of **95 to 101 percent** of the theoretical Nernst response, which corresponds to **56.2 to 59.8 mV/pH unit at 25 °C** 【6†"Properly working electrodes should have slopes that are 56.2 to 59.8 mV/pH unit at 25 °C, which is 95 to 101 percent"】.
- The ideal slope at 25 °C is 59.16 mV/pH unit 【3†"The ideal slope of the calibration curve at 25 °C, based on the Nernst equation (see section 2.2), is 59.16 mV/pH unit"】.

**If it fails:** a slope outside 95–101 percent indicates probable electrode deterioration 【12†"slope of less than 95 percent or greater than 101 percent indicates probable electrode deterioration"】. The guidance is to first clean the electrode and check the filling-solution level, that the fill hole is open, and that the junction is free flowing, then recalibrate 【11†"first clean the electrode and check: the level of the filling solution, that the fill hole is open, and that the junction is free flowing; then, recalibrate"】. If it still fails after recalibration, the electrode should be cleaned, reconditioned, or replaced 【7†"Clean, recondition, or replace the electrode if, after recalibration, the slope remains outside the acceptable range of 95 to 101 percent"】.

One more relevant note for your situation: the typical useful life expectancy of pH electrodes in environmental field operation is approximately 12 to 18 months, so a two-season-old electrode is worth watching closely 【19†"the typical useful life expectancy of pH electrodes used in environmental field operation is approximately 12 to 18 months"】. Your sluggish response is also consistent with what the troubleshooting guide lists as a possible cause of slow response, including a clogged or partially clogged junction or a contaminated electrode 【8†"Clogged or partially clogged junction—follow the manufacturer's instructions to unclog the junction"】.

turns.answer:
A slope of 92 percent is below the acceptable range, so the electrode is not passing as-is. Here's the sequence the guidance gives:

**1. Clean and check first, then recalibrate.** If the slope is outside the acceptable range, first clean the electrode and check the level of the filling solution, that the fill hole is open, and that the junction is free flowing; then recalibrate 【11†"first clean the electrode and check: the level of the filling solution, that the fill hole is open, and that the junction is free flowing; then, recalibrate"】. Routine cleaning options include soaking in 0.1-M HCl for 30 minutes to remove solid precipitates fouling the reference junction, or a dilute bleach soak for bacterial contaminants — rinsing thoroughly with DIW before use or storage 【10†"Soak the electrode (whether gel- or liquid-filled) in 0.1-M HCl for 30 minutes"】.

**2. If it's a liquid-filled electrode, recondition it.** Try reconditioning it in the laboratory before replacing it with a new electrode 【12†"If a liquid-filled electrode is being used, try reconditioning it (section 3.2) in the laboratory before replacing it with a new electrode"】. That means flushing and refilling the filling solution, since salt crystal deposits in the reference electrode or reference junction commonly cause pH electrodes to malfunction 【1†"Salt crystal deposits in the reference electrode or reference junction commonly cause pH electrodes to malfunction"】.

**3. When to order a new one.** Clean, recondition, or replace the electrode if, after recalibration, the slope remains outside the acceptable range of 95 to 101 percent 【7†"Clean, recondition, or replace the electrode if, after recalibration, the slope remains outside the acceptable range of 95 to 101 percent"】. So: if you've cleaned it, reconditioned it, and the slope still won't come back into 95–101 percent, that's the point to replace it.

Two things worth noting given your probe's age and sluggishness: a slope of less than 95 percent indicates probable electrode deterioration 【12†"slope of less than 95 percent or greater than 101 percent indicates probable electrode deterioration"】, and slow response times may indicate reduced electrode performance or a clogged reference junction 【10†"Slow response times may indicate reduced electrode performance or a clogged reference junction"】. Also, the typical useful life expectancy of pH electrodes used in environmental field operation is approximately 12 to 18 months 【19†"the typical useful life expectancy of pH electrodes used in environmental field operation is approximately 12 to 18 months"】 — at two seasons, yours is at or past that, so even a successful reconditioning may only buy you limited time.

• a thermistor that functions properly and accurately
measures the temperature

tures to verify the accuracy of the readings. Recalibration
may be necessary if the initial check is more than ±0.05 pH
unit different from the value the buffer should return. If the
measurement temperature is more than ±10 °C different from
the laboratory calibration temperature, checks in the field are
more likely to fail and recalibration may be necessary.
The following guidelines and standard procedures
generally apply whenever a pH instrument system is to be
calibrated. Because calibration and operating procedures can
differ with the instrument system, check the manufacturer’s
recommended calibration procedures and calibration buffer
solution requirements. Modern pH meters typically compen-
sate for buffer temperatures automatically during calibration.
When using these instruments, follow the manufacturer’s
calibration instructions and the more general instructions in
the following procedures—do not take shortcuts.
• Before each field trip and site visit, check pH-meter/
electrode logbook records for electrode performance.
Remember—any noted calibration slope of less
than 95 percent or greater than 101 percent indicates
probable electrode deterioration. If the slope is outside
the acceptable range (95–101 percent), the electrode
should be cleaned, reconditioned, or replaced, and the
new electrode calibrated. If a liquid-filled electrode is
being used, try reconditioning it (section 3.2) in the
laboratory before replacing it with a new electrode.

Step 4. Recheck instrument calibration.
Check the stability of the pH meter and electrode in the
field by measuring the pH of the buffer whose pH is nearest
to that of the samples. If the pH of the buffer differs by more
than 0.05 pH units from the certified value at the measured
temperature (table 6.4–3), recalibrate the pH system and then
remeasure the pH of the sample.
5.2 	Measurement of pH in Waters with Low
Specific Conductance
Accurate and precise measurement of pH in low-specific-
conductance waters (less than 100 μS/cm) is challenging
because (1) the water is not sufficiently conductive to complete
the electrical circuit and allow for a stable pH reading using
a combination pH electrode, (2) differences in ionic strength
between the sample and buffers are large, and (3) the potential
of the liquid junction is larger than normal. Modern reference
junctions are designed to decrease the effects of low specific
conductance, but may not always produce the desired accuracy
for measurements of pH. Low-resistance glass pH electrodes
or reference junctions with a fast, continuous leak rate can
be used to make accurate measurements of pH in low-ionic-
strength waters; however, because these electrodes are expen-
sive, generally are not designed for fieldwork, and only work
well in dilute waters, they do not replace traditional electrodes.
Some methods recommend calibrating with low-ionic-strength
buffers to minimize liquid junction potential errors, but these
buffers are easily contaminated and should be avoided in
field settings.
The recommended method allows for using normal
pH field electrodes and standard pH buffers (table 6.4–3)
by adding a small amount of potassium chloride (KCl) to a
subsample of water to increase the specific conductance by
approximately 150 μS/cm. Increasing the specific conduc-
tance by this amount has little effect on the hydrogen ion
activity coefficient; the pH is expected to be affected by less
than 0.01 pH units (Busenberg and Plummer, 1987). It is first
recommended to determine the pH by using the procedures
described in section 5.1. If the sample pH does not stabilize,
and the specific conductance is less than 100 μS/cm, then the
following procedure is recommended:
1. 	Before going to the field, prepare small glass vials
containing 20 milligrams (mg) of dry potassium chlo-
ride (KCl—crystalline, American Chemical Society-
certified). Prepare more vials than the expected number
of pH measurements. (Note: Addition of other salts [for
example, sodium chloride] also will increase the specific
conductance, but KCl is recommended to minimize
effects on the liquid junction potential.)

raw sample water. Immediately transfer 20 mg KCl to
the sample solution, cap the solution to minimize trans-
fer of gases, and gently swirl the bottle to dissolve the
KCl. Maintain the sample at ambient temperature. This
procedure will increase the specific conductance of the
sample by approximately 150 μS/cm.

A slope of 92 percent is below the acceptable range, so the electrode is not passing as-is. Here's the sequence the guidance gives:

**1. Clean and check first, then recalibrate.** If the slope is outside the acceptable range, first clean the electrode and check the level of the filling solution, that the fill hole is open, and that the junction is free flowing; then recalibrate 【11†"first clean the electrode and check: the level of the filling solution, that the fill hole is open, and that the junction is free flowing; then, recalibrate"】. Routine cleaning options include soaking in 0.1-M HCl for 30 minutes to remove solid precipitates fouling the reference junction, or a dilute bleach soak for bacterial contaminants — rinsing thoroughly with DIW before use or storage 【10†"Soak the electrode (whether gel- or liquid-filled) in 0.1-M HCl for 30 minutes"】.

**2. If it's a liquid-filled electrode, recondition it.** Try reconditioning it in the laboratory before replacing it with a new electrode 【12†"If a liquid-filled electrode is being used, try reconditioning it (section 3.2) in the laboratory before replacing it with a new electrode"】. That means flushing and refilling the filling solution, since salt crystal deposits in the reference electrode or reference junction commonly cause pH electrodes to malfunction 【1†"Salt crystal deposits in the reference electrode or reference junction commonly cause pH electrodes to malfunction"】.

**3. When to order a new one.** Clean, recondition, or replace the electrode if, after recalibration, the slope remains outside the acceptable range of 95 to 101 percent 【7†"Clean, recondition, or replace the electrode if, after recalibration, the slope remains outside the acceptable range of 95 to 101 percent"】. So: if you've cleaned it, reconditioned it, and the slope still won't come back into 95–101 percent, that's the point to replace it.

Two things worth noting given your probe's age and sluggishness: a slope of less than 95 percent indicates probable electrode deterioration 【12†"slope of less than 95 percent or greater than 101 percent indicates probable electrode deterioration"】, and slow response times may indicate reduced electrode performance or a clogged reference junction 【10†"Slow response times may indicate reduced electrode performance or a clogged reference junction"】. Also, the typical useful life expectancy of pH electrodes used in environmental field operation is approximately 12 to 18 months 【19†"the typical useful life expectancy of pH electrodes used in environmental field operation is approximately 12 to 18 months"】 — at two seasons, yours is at or past that, so even a successful reconditioning may only buy you limited time.
